drafts.notes:
My angle was fidelity to the MEC. I checked the capacity in the uploaded Priorización curricular 2021 (Comunicación Guaraní, 1.º grado, item 16 «pedir ayuda, favor, permiso, préstamo de algún objeto o material» and item 18 «expresiones de cortesía en sus diálogos», p. 28). I also checked the 2021 planning guide (weeks C–D, pp. 50–51: «Vocabulario básico. Expresión de necesidades básicas», «Presentación de elementos de uso cotidiano en el aula»; week 15, p. 54: «pedir permiso, solicitar algún objeto y agradecer»). Neither document gives any Guarani wording, so the Guarani is mine.

How the unit maps to the MEC:
- Night 1, with the teacher: pedir ayuda (Ndaikatúi says why, then Chepytyvõ / Chepytyvõmína) and pedir un favor (Eipe'amína ovetã).
- Night 2, at the classroom door: pedir permiso with one reusable frame, Ikatúpa + a-verb? (aike, aguapy, añembosarái). The teacher answers Héẽ, eike, which also covers item 4, understanding courtesy words.
- Night 3, with a classmate (irũ): préstamo of an object (Reiporukápa chéve nde haiha?) and of material (Eme'ẽmína chéve kuatia), then thanks (Aguyjevete).
- Thanking comes up every night. Each night's say lines are a short polite exchange (request, answer, thanks), which is item 18.

A 6-year-old leaves with three reusable tools: -mína = «por favor», Ikatúpa…? = «¿puedo…?», and Aguyje / Aguyjevete = «gracias». The 2.º grado needs (baño, tomar agua, pedir alimentos) are left out on purpose.

Reuse:
- Words with unchanged meanings: Aguyje (gloss 'Gracias'), irũ ('amiga, amigo'), mbo'ehára (in the say lines), haiha and kuatia (inside phrases), and the verb of unit 4's Ñañembosarái.
- Existing pictures, which give the MEC's «elementos de uso cotidiano en el aula»: okẽ, ovetã, apyka, pelota, haiha, kuatia, irũ, aguyje.
- Only 2 new pictures: ndaikatúi and pytyvõ.
- The aguyje heart serves both Aguyje (night 1) and Aguyjevete (night 3), in different nights.
- In the guessing games the engine never puts a phrase next to a card for a word it contains, or two cards with the same picture. So «Reiporukápa chéve nde haiha?» never appears next to unit 4's «haiha», nor «…kuatia» next to «kuatia».

Games per track:
- L2: meet, pick, say every night.
- BI: meet, then pick or read, then say.
- L1, night 1: builds Ndaikatúi, Chepytyvõ and Aguyje (the first three items with syllables).
- L1, night 2: plays pairs with the three Ikatúpa phrases (door, chair, ball).
- L1, night 3: builds irũ and Aguyjevete.

Card order follows a small story for the meet game. The existing clips for Aguyje and irũ can be reused; everything else needs new clips. Night 3's two request cards are about 10 syllables, a little longer than any card in the app now (the longest are about 9).

doubts.doubt: poruka 'prestar' (poru 'usar' + -uka) is the dictionary and school form (Guasch & Ortiz; jeporuka 'préstamo'), but I found it in no MEC text. Everyday speech often uses the colloquial puru- (reipurukápa) or Spanish presta. I am fairly sure of the i- (reiporuka, like reiporu), and less sure it is the verb a Paraguayan teacher would pick first. If a speaker objects, this keeps the picture and repeats the night-2 frame: «Ikatúpa aiporu nde haiha?» (¿Puedo usar tu lápiz?).

-mína (-mi + -na) is the usual Guarani way to say 'por favor' in a request. I write it with the accent on mí because -na is atonic (as in ejumína). Some speakers would rather say «Chepytyvõmi» or «Eipytyvõmína chéve». Chepytyvõ as the imperative 'ayudame' (che- for the object, no e-) is standard.
«Héẽ» ('sí') is the spelling in most school and course material, but «Hẽe» is also seen. Please confirm the Academia's form, since this would be the first time the app writes it.

I split it Ndai·ka·túi, keeping the diphthongs together as the app does (Mai·tei, hai·ha, 'éi). A teacher could split it Nda·i·ka·tú·i. The word means both 'no puedo' and 'no se puede'. The new picture (a child who cannot reach a shelf) shows only one case of it.

I use eipyhy ('agarrá', from pyhy 'agarrar, tomar') as the answer when handing something over. Some speakers say «ejapyhy». If a reviewer finds it odd, «Héẽ.» alone or «Héẽ, eiporu.» (Sí, usalo) also works.

Guarani has no article, so the gloss «una hoja» adds 'una' (kuatia = papel, hoja). At about 10 syllables, this card and «Reiporukápa chéve nde haiha?» are longer than any card in the app now. «Eme'ẽmi chéve kuatia» is one syllable shorter but less clearly 'por favor'.

It is correct and natural, but asking to sit down happens less often in class than asking to come in or to play. An alternative with an existing picture is «Ikatúpa ahecha?» (¿Puedo ver?, picture resa). «Ikatúpa añembosarái?» is about 9 syllables long.
irũ and mbo'ehára have no gender. The say glosses use «amiga» and «maestra» and could just as well say «amigo» and «maestro». The cards keep the app's 'amiga, amigo' and 'maestra, maestro'.

drafts.notes:
I built this unit for 1.º grado from the MEC's Priorización curricular 2021, Comunicación Guaraní (the L2 table): item 16 (ayuda, favor, permiso, préstamo) and item 18 (cortesía). It follows the situations in the 2021 planning guide.

Each night is one classroom situation. Its «say» is a three-line mini dialogue, and the child says every line: the request, the answer (always starting with Héẽ), then the thanks.
- Night 1, talking to the teacher (help): Mbo'ehára, chepytyvõmína → Héẽ, roipytyvõta → Aguyje!
- Night 2, talking to the teacher (permission): one pattern, Ikatúpa + a verb in the first person (aike, aguapy, ahecha, añembosarái). Each uses an existing picture: door, chair, eye, ball. Dialogue: Ikatúpa aike? → Héẽ, eike. Eguapy → Aguyje, mbo'ehára.
- Night 3, talking to a classmate (borrowing and asking for material, the guide's «solicitar algún objeto»): Eiporuka chéve nde haiha → Héẽ, ejapyhy → Aguyjevete!

Courtesy forms taught: the request suffix -mína («por favor»), Ikatúpa? («¿puedo?», «¿se puede?»), Aguyje and Aguyjevete. Héẽ («sí») is new to the app and opens every answer.
- I chose -mína over the school translations of «por favor», Nde py'aporãrõ and Ikatúrõ. Both are longer and seldom said to a 6-year-old.
- I left out «de nada» because I am not sure which form is standard.

Reused with the same meaning, gloss, picture and syllables they have in the app: mbo'ehára and irũ (the two people the child talks to), Aguyje, haiha and kuatia. Two verbs are also reused: ñembosarái (as in Ñañembosarái!, with the same ball picture) and hecha (as in the Meet title Ehecha ha ehendu).

Left out on purpose: Spanish loanwords common in mixed Guarani-Spanish speech (embopresta, ajuga, por favor), and the needs 2.º grado adds (baño, agua, comida).

Pictures: 2 new ones, pytyvõ and héẽ. Both keys are free in project/tp-pics.js. All reused keys exist in the same Unicode form, and each syllable list joins back to its word.

I ran the unit in memory through the real engine, project/tp-course.js, placed after unit 4. No file was written.
- Pick and Check only drew distractors from this unit's 10 different pictures. So Aguyje and Aguyjevete never appear together, and héẽ never appears next to iporã's thumbs-up.
- Games per night: L1 meet+read+build | meet+read+pairs | meet+read+build. L2 meet+pick+say on all three nights. BI meet+pick+say | meet+read+say | meet+pick+say.
- Syllables are given for the 4 one-word items of night 1 and the 2 of night 3. Night 2 is all phrases and needs none.
- The say lines «Aguyje!» and «Aguyjevete!» use the same sound keys as the word items, so those voice clips are shared.

Placement: the unit uses unit 4's school words, so it fits right after «Che mbo'ehao». One structural problem: 1.º grado has 7 units for Eichu's 7 stars. The header of project/tp-grades.js and project/tp-sky.js both say one star per unit. An 8th unit breaks that rule unless two units are merged or the figure changes.

doubts.doubt: poruka («prestar», from poru «usar» + -ka) is the Guarani verb. The MEC's own Guarani text writes both oiporu and oipuru, so some children will hear «eipuruka». Many Guarani-speaking families actually say the Spanish-loan «Embopresta chéve…». A Guarani teacher should confirm that 1.º grado classes use «eiporuka». The fallback is «Eme'ẽmína chéve nde haiha» (pasame tu lápiz).

I write the courtesy suffix joined to the verb and with an accent, as in chepytyvõmína and eme'ẽmína. Some materials write -mina. In everyday speech the shorter -mi (chepytyvõmi) is at least as common. The Academia spelling and which form teachers prefer still need to be confirmed. The same goes for writing chepytyvõ as one word, which I believe is standard but some write as «che pytyvõ».

The Academia spelling is héẽ, two syllables (hé-ẽ); «hẽe» and «heẽ» are also seen. The synthetic voice may not pronounce the nasal second vowel well, so its clip needs checking. Its new picture (a check mark with a nodding face) must not look like iporã's thumbs-up. The games only ever compare it with this unit's pictures.
My best guess at the everyday word for «tomá» when handing something over is «Ejapyhy» (agarrá). Some speakers would just say «Ko'ápe» (acá está).

The ro- prefix (yo a vos) is new grammar for an L2 child. If it proves hard to repeat, «Héẽ, roipytyvõ» (no -ta) is shorter and still means «sí, te ayudo». I am not sure which reply teachers use most.
As far as I know, «Eike, eguapy» (pasá, sentate) is the usual welcome. It still needs a check that it sounds natural from a teacher to a pupil, not only from a host to a guest.
I kept the app's verb (Ñañembosarái!), but many children say «Ikatúpa ajuga?», with the Spanish loanword.

I glossed the address as «Profe»: it is what Paraguayan children call a teacher, and it works for a man or a woman. If the app should stick to its own gloss of mbo'ehára, use «Maestra». Also, children often say «Profe» even when speaking Guarani, so «Mbo'ehára» as a form of address is the school way, not always the everyday one.
Without «peteĩ» it means «dame papel» or «dame una hoja». «Eme'ẽmína chéve peteĩ kuatia» says «una hoja» exactly but is longer.
The plain door picture (okẽ) stands for «¿Puedo pasar?». A new picture of a child at a half-open door would show it better, which would make it the third new picture.

merged.notes:
This unit merges the two drafts. Where both drafts agreed, their Guarani is kept unchanged.

Kept from both drafts:
- the unit title Ikatúpa?
- Chepytyvõ, with the new helping-hands picture, and Aguyje
- the night-2 frame Ikatúpa + a-verb? (aike, aguapy, añembosarái)
- irũ, the pencil request with poruka, Eme'ẽmína chéve kuatia, and Aguyjevete on the aguyje heart
- Héẽ at the start of every answer

Where the drafts differed:
- Night 1 takes mbo'ehára from Draft 2 (the person the child asks; it mirrors irũ in night 3). It takes Eipe'amína ovetã from Draft 1, the MEC's «favor», which Draft 2 did not cover.
- Two cards are left out:
  - Draft 1's Ndaikatúi: its picture, a child who cannot reach a shelf, would also read as «ayudame» next to the helping hands.
  - Draft 2's Héẽ: its picture (a check mark and a nodding face) is abstract and close to the iporã thumbs-up. Also, the synthetic voice garbles short nasal words (irũ, okẽ and akã are held back). Héẽ is still said in all three dialogues.
- Night 2 takes Draft 2's fourth card, Ikatúpa ahecha? (Draft 1 listed it as an alternative). It also takes Draft 2's dialogue: «Héẽ, eike. Eguapy.» links the answer to the aguapy card.
- Night 3 keeps Draft 1's question «Reiporukápa chéve nde haiha?» rather than Draft 2's imperative «Eiporuka chéve nde haiha». The imperative has no -mína, so it is less polite, and «Héẽ» answers a question more naturally. The answer uses ejapyhy, which both drafts name. The closing line, «Aguyjevete, che irũ!», comes from Draft 1 and uses the night's irũ.
- Glosses:
  - «Maestra» (the app's gloss of mbo'ehára) is used rather than «Profe».
  - All four night-2 glosses start with «¿Puedo…?», so the child maps Ikatúpa to one Spanish frame.

Fit with the MEC (Priorización curricular 2021, Comunicación Guaraní, 1.º grado, items 16 and 18; 2021 planning guide):
- Night 1, with the teacher: pedir ayuda and pedir un favor.
- Night 2, at the classroom door: pedir permiso.
- Night 3, with a classmate: préstamo of an object (haiha) and of material (kuatia).
- Every night ends with thanks, and each say set is a request, an answer and a thank-you («práctica oral simulada», item 18).
- The courtesy tools taught are -mína, Ikatúpa…? and Aguyje / Aguyjevete.
- The 2.º grado needs (baño, agua, comida) are left out.

Checked in memory against project/tp-course.js, with the unit placed after unit 4:
- Every syl list joins back to its word.
- Every reused picture key exists, in the same Unicode form, and the pictures are distinct within each night. There is only one new picture, pytyvõ.

  - L2: meet+pick+say on all three nights.
  - BI: meet+pick+say | meet+read+say | meet+pick+say.
- All Pick and Check distractors come from this unit. Aguyje and Aguyjevete never appear together, and no phrase appears next to a word it contains.
- A playthrough of the whole grade on L1, L2 and BI lights 8 of 8 units.
- Clips: the unit needs 18 keys.
  - «Aguyje!», «Ikatúpa aike?» and «Reiporukápa chéve nde haiha?» share their card's clip.

All 25 Guarani strings pass the spelling and syllable check, so this lens needs no fix and no drop. Nothing was edited.

SYLLABLES: The five syl lists (mbo'ehára, Chepytyvõ, Aguyje, irũ, Aguyjevete) each join exactly to their gn. Every syllable ends in a vowel, ch and mb are kept whole, and the puso begins its syllable. All multi-word items have []. Every string is NFC with the ASCII puso. ACCENT RULE AS APPLIED:
- Atonic suffixes in this unit: the question -pa (Ikatúpa, Reiporukápa), the future -ta (roipytyvõta), the request -na (-mína) and the dative -ve (chéve).
- Tonic suffixes: the courtesy -mi (hence -mína), -vete (Aguyjevete, no accent, like the app's porãite), and the agentive -hára (accented on há).
- An oral stressed vowel that is no longer last takes the acute: Ikatúpa, Reiporukápa, chéve, -mína.
- A nasal stressed vowel takes no acute before an atonic suffix, because the tilde marks the stress: roipytyvõta, like the app's Moõpa?.
- A root keeps its tilde when the stress moves to a tonic suffix: Chepytyvõmína, Eme'ẽmína, like the app's Mokõivéva and ñe'ẽtéva.

WORD BOUNDARIES AND NASAL HARMONY: che- joins the verb when it is the object prefix (Chepytyvõ) and is written apart when it is a possessive (che irũ, nde haiha). chéve is one word. -pa, -ta, -mína and -vete are written joined. nde stays nde before oral haiha. The reflexive is ñe- before mb (añembosarái). che has no nasal form.

Result: all 25 Guarani strings are grammatical, and each means what its Spanish says. I found no fix or drop under this lens. Nothing in any project file was changed.

What I checked:
- Verb person: Chepytyvõ uses che- with no e- (2sg acting on 1sg). roipytyvõta uses ro- (yo → vos) and keeps the i- of an i-verb, as in ndaroikuaái. Every imperative is 2sg e- for one listener (eipe'a, eme'ẽ, eike, eguapy, ejapyhy). The permission frame is Ikatúpa + a 1sg a- verb (aike, aguapy, ahecha, añembosarái).
- Recipient and possessives: chéve marks the receiver with me'ẽ and poruka; nde haiha and che irũ are right.
- Suffixes: -mína is joined, with the accent on mí. -pa is atonic, which gives Ikatúpa and Reiporukápa. -ta is glossed with a Spanish present, as the app already does (Jajotopáta = «¡Nos vemos!»).
- Negation: none is used, since Ndaikatúi was dropped.
- Dialogues: each night's say set is a request, a fitting Héẽ answer, and thanks.
- Meanings in the app: no reused word changes meaning (mbo'ehára, irũ, Aguyje, haiha, kuatia, ovetã, añembosarái). None of the new forms (Héẽ, pytyvõ, poruka, japyhy, ikatu, eike, guapy, pe'a, me'ẽ, -mína, chéve, Aguyjevete) appears anywhere else in the app's data or screens, so nothing clashes. No false friends.
- Glosses: they are short and in voseo. The titles' Spanish lines name the topic rather than translate, which is the app's pattern and was accepted in the earlier audit.

Advice on the doubts:
- Keep Chepytyvõmína. Don't switch to «Eipytyvõmína chéve», which is a Spanish-style calque.
- Keep -ta in roipytyvõta, and keep the gloss «Sí, te ayudo.».

What is left is word choice and spelling, not grammar:

verdicts.general:
Overall the unit is natural, polite and current school Guarani that a Paraguayan teacher would model for 6-year-olds. It has no needless jopara (no «por favor», «presta», «juga» or «profe») and no invented words; every verb is traditional (pytyvõ, pe'a, me'ẽ, ike, guapy, hecha, ñembosarái, japyhy, poru/poruka).

Attested online (some exactly, some as patterns):
- «¡Chepytyvõmína!» and «Chepytyvõ!».
- The frame «Ikatúpa + a-verb?» («Ikatúpa asẽ sapy'aite», «Ikatúpa aipuru nde haiha?»).
- «roipytyvõta» (Biblia GPC 2006, Éx 4:12).
- «Eike, eguapy», «Aguyjevete», «Eme'ẽ chéve…».
The rest are plausible but unattested combinations of attested parts; I found none doubtful except as noted below.

Spelling of -mína: the accent on mí is confirmed by ABC Color (ejúna / ejumi / ejúke / ejumína), so Chepytyvõmína, Eipe'amína and Eme'ẽmína are right. Héẽ is the most common school spelling, but variants (hẽe, heẽ) exist and I found no Academia page online to settle it.

One change recommended: replace «Reiporukápa chéve nde haiha?» (card and say line) with «Ikatúpa aiporu nde haiha?» (¿Puedo usar tu lápiz?). It is attested near-verbatim on Tatoeba and reuses night 2's frame, which makes it easier for an L2 child. Keep the original only if the team wants the explicit verb 'prestar'; it is grammatical and its accent is right. Optionally answer «Héẽ, eiporu.» instead of «Héẽ, ejapyhy.» (both are fine). On usage grounds, «Ikatúpa ahecha?» is the least typical card in night 2.

MEC corpus (scratchpad mec-text): none of the unit's Guarani phrases appear in it, because these texts contain little Guarani.
- It confirms the capacities: Guía para la planificación 2021, 1.er ciclo, Comunicación Guaraní 1.º grado, p.50-51 and p.54 (25531b74 l.2385-2402 and 2543-2556).
- It confirms the expected courtesy repertoire: 1.º grado guide «permiso, gracias, buenos días…» (4453a06b l.1990); 2.º grado guide «Con permiso», «Me permite», «¡Muchas gracias», «¡Por favor!» (8344c61a l.513).
- It attests related forms: «Eiporu», «Eiporuporã», «ojeporu» (MAGUA teacher guides); «Oipuru» (Priorización 2021); «Echutána», «Emoingéke» (6.º grado guide, with the accent before atonic -na and -ke); «tomoguahẽmi oréve» (-mi as a polite softener, Pages_from_4933 l.229); «mbo’ehára»; «ikatúta».

-mína (-mi + -na) is the usual courtesy ending «por favor». The usage lens found «¡Chepytyvõmína!» = «Ayuda, por favor» in the ASU2025 Guarani booklet. Tatoeba writes the courtesy -mi with the accent before atonic endings (Eikemíkena, Eme'ẽmíkena, Eguahẽmíkena, ikatumína), so Chepytyvõmína, Eipe'amína and Eme'ẽmína follow one rule. Still to confirm: the Academia's spelling. Some materials write -mina, and if the acute were ruled out, all four -mína strings would change together. In speech, -mi alone (chepytyvõmi) and -míkena are also common. The meaning lens advises against «Eipytyvõmína chéve», a Spanish-style calque. The object prefix is written joined (Chepytyvõ), but the possessive che is written apart (che irũ), and L1 readers will meet both.

Héẽ ('sí') opens all three answers and is new to the app. Tatoeba has both «Héẽ.» and «Hẽe.» for «Yes.», and Omniglot has «Hêe». The strict rule (a tilde only on the stressed nasal vowel) would give hẽe or heẽ. I kept Héẽ, the spelling in most school material and in the Regensburg transcripts. Please confirm the Academia's dictionary entry. The synthetic voice has garbled short nasal words (irũ, okẽ and akã are held back), so check the three clips that begin with Héẽ.

It is correct and attested: «Che roipytyvõta» (Biblia GPC 2006, Éx 4:12, found by the usage lens). But the ro- prefix (yo a vos) is new grammar for an L2 child. If it proves hard to repeat, «Héẽ, roipytyvõ» (no -ta) is shorter and still means «sí, te ayudo». The gloss «Sí, te ayudo.» renders the future -ta freely, as the app does with Jajotopáta (¡Nos vemos!).

The gloss «Maestra» follows the app's gloss of mbo'ehára. Paraguayan children say «Profe», which works for a man or a woman, often even when speaking Guarani. So «Mbo'ehára» as a form of address is the school way, not always the everyday one.

Two lenses found it natural. «Eike, eguapy» (pasá, sentate) is the usual welcome, attested in a vocabulary list, and it fits a teacher talking to one pupil. The only open point is whether a teacher would soften it to «Eguapymi». «Héẽ, eike.» alone is the simpler fallback.

All three lenses passed «Ejapyhy» ('agarrá, tomá') for handing something over, but no source I could reach shows it in this exact use. «Eipyhy» is also correct, and others would just say «Ko'ápe» or «Héẽ.». Now that the card is «Ikatúpa aiporu nde haiha?», «Héẽ, eiporu.» (Sí, usalo) would mirror it the way «Héẽ, eike.» mirrors «Ikatúpa aike?». The usage lens offers it as an option. It is not applied, because no lens marked ejapyhy wrong.

Guarani has no article, so the gloss adds «una»; in the app, kuatia is 'hoja de papel'. «Eme'ẽmína chéve peteĩ kuatia» says «una hoja» exactly but is longer. Tatoeba's «Eme'ẽmíkena chéve…» (Please give me…) supports the pattern. At 22 characters it is also longer than any card the app has now.

pe'a is the verb children learn first for opening a door or window; mbojuruja also exists. A child more often asks a classmate, or asks permission to open the window («Ikatúpa aipe'a ovetã?», suggested by the usage lens). As a favour asked of the teacher it is natural, but a reviewer may prefer one of those.
The plain closed door (okẽ) stands for «¿Puedo pasar?». A new picture of a child at a half-open door would show it better. It would be the unit's second new picture.

The usage lens calls it the least typical request in class, and so the first card to cut if night 2 goes down to three. It is still natural Guarani: Tatoeba has «Ikatu piko ahecha?» (Can I see?) and «Ikatúpa rehecha?». It came from Draft 2 only.

It is correct and natural, but asking to sit down happens less often in class than asking to come in or to play. Its value is that it sets up the teacher's «Eguapy». It keeps the app's verb (Ñañembosarái!), but many children say «Ikatúpa ajuga?», with the Spanish loanword.
irũ and mbo'ehára have no gender. The say glosses use «amiga» and «maestra» and could just as well say «amigo» and «maestro». The cards keep the app's 'amiga, amigo' and 'maestra, maestro'.
